claim: Drosophila larvae are innately attracted by most volatile molecules.
source: Drosophila larvae are innately attracted by most volatile molecules (Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005; Kreher et al., 2008; Mathew et al., 2013), and repelled by a few, such as CO2 (Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Drosophila larvae are repelled by CO2.
source: Drosophila larvae are innately attracted by most volatile molecules (Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005; Kreher et al., 2008; Mathew et al., 2013), and repelled by a few, such as CO2 (Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Larvae navigate gradients of innately attractive or repulsive odors via klinotaxis.
source: Larvae navigate gradients of innately attractive or repulsive odors via klinotaxis (Gershow et al., 2012; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012; Schulze et al., 2015; Gepner et al., 2015), by modulating turning and crawling in response to changes in odor concentration.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Larvae modulate turning and crawling in response to changes in odor concentration.
source: Larvae navigate gradients of innately attractive or repulsive odors via klinotaxis (Gershow et al., 2012; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012; Schulze et al., 2015; Gepner et al., 2015), by modulating turning and crawling in response to changes in odor concentration.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Associative odor learning has been shown to modify the turning response to odor.
source: Associative odor learning has been shown to modify the turning response to odor (Schleyer et al., 2015; Paisios et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: After the innately attractive odor was paired with optogenetic punishment, larvae no longer approached it, and instead avoided it.
source: As expected, we found that after the innately attractive odor was paired with optogenetic punishment, on average, larvae no longer approached it, and instead avoided it (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Following unpaired odor presentation, the navigation index reached +0.1.
source: Following unpaired odor presentation this index reached +0.1, that is similar to previous studies looking at naive larvae navigating toward ethyl acetate, at this dilution (Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and comparison to prior research

claim: Following odor presentation paired with Basin activation, the navigation index reached –0.1.
source: Following odor presentation paired with Basin activation, the index reached –0.1, that is similar to larvae navigating away from CO2 (Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and comparison to prior research

claim: The paired group turned more when crawling up the odor gradient, than down the odor gradient, whereas the unpaired group larvae did the opposite.
source: This involved a change in the coupling between odor intensity change and turn probability: the paired group turned more when crawling up the odor gradient, than down the odor gradient, whereas the unpaired group larvae did the opposite (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c

claim: Some MBONs encode positive valence, while others encode negative valence.
source: Based on studies in the adult (Aso et al., 2014b), we hypothesized that some MBONs encode positive valence, while others encode negative valence.
evidence: Hypothesis based on prior research in adult Drosophila

claim: A neuron whose activation signals positive valence is expected to suppress turning in response to an increase in its activity.
source: A neuron whose activation signals positive valence is therefore expected to suppress turning in response to an increase in its activity, and promote turning in response to a decrease in its activity.
evidence: Logical inference from the definition of positive valence and larval navigation behavior

claim: A neuron whose activation signals negative valence is expected to promote turning in response to an increase in its activity.
source: Conversely, a neuron whose activation signals negative valence (avoidance) is expected to promote turning in response to an increase in its activity.
evidence: Logical inference from the definition of negative valence and larval navigation behavior

claim: Activating MBON-a1 induced approach behavior.
source: Activating the two calyx-MBONs induced opposite responses: approach and avoidance, for MBON-a1 (Nexp = 7, Nlarvae = 250) and MBON-a2 (Nexp = 7, Nlarvae = 280), respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: Activating MBON-a2 induced avoidance behavior.
source: Activating the two calyx-MBONs induced opposite responses: approach and avoidance, for MBON-a1 (Nexp = 7, Nlarvae = 250) and MBON-a2 (Nexp = 7, Nlarvae = 280), respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: Activating MBON-b1/b2 together induced approach behavior.
source: Activating peduncle-MBONs, MBON-b1/b2 together (Nexp = 8, Nlarvae = 340) induced approach.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c

claim: Activating MBON-h1/h2 induced avoidance behavior.
source: Activating medial lobe MBONs induced avoidance: MBON-h1/h2 (Nexp = 10, Nlarvae = 450), MBON-i1 (Nexp = 6, Nlarvae = 240), and MBON-k1 (Nexp = 6, Nlarvae = 210).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d

claim: Activating MBON-i1 induced avoidance behavior.
source: Activating medial lobe MBONs induced avoidance: MBON-h1/h2 (Nexp = 10, Nlarvae = 450), MBON-i1 (Nexp = 6, Nlarvae = 240), and MBON-k1 (Nexp = 6, Nlarvae = 210).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d

claim: Activating MBON-k1 induced avoidance behavior.
source: Activating medial lobe MBONs induced avoidance: MBON-h1/h2 (Nexp = 10, Nlarvae = 450), MBON-i1 (Nexp = 6, Nlarvae = 240), and MBON-k1 (Nexp = 6, Nlarvae = 210).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d

claim: Activating MBON-d1 induced approach behavior.
source: Activating the lateral appendix-MBON-d1 (Nexp = 9, Nlarvae = 250) induced approach.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e

claim: Activating MBON-g1/g2 induced approach behavior.
source: Activating the vertical lobe-MBONs induced approach: MBON-g1/g2 (Nexp = 6, Nlarvae = 210) and MBON-m1 (Nexp = 9, Nlarvae = 450).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f

claim: Activating MBON-m1 induced approach behavior.
source: Activating the vertical lobe-MBONs induced approach: MBON-g1/g2 (Nexp = 6, Nlarvae = 210) and MBON-m1 (Nexp = 9, Nlarvae = 450).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f

claim: Activating MBON-e2 induced avoidance behavior.
source: Activating the two MBONs in the tip of vertical lobe had opposite effects: MBON-e2 (Nexp = 5, Nlarvae = 140) and -e1 (Nexp = 6, Nlarvae = 250, using tsh-GAL80 to eliminate nerve cord expression) induced avoidance- and approach-like responses, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g

claim: Activating MBON-e1 induced approach behavior.
source: Activating the two MBONs in the tip of vertical lobe had opposite effects: MBON-e2 (Nexp = 5, Nlarvae = 140) and -e1 (Nexp = 6, Nlarvae = 250, using tsh-GAL80 to eliminate nerve cord expression) induced avoidance- and approach-like responses, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g

claim: Most negative-valence MBONs innervate appetitive-memory compartments.
source: Note that most negative-valence MBONs innervate appetitive-memory com- partments (3/5), and the remainder innervate compartment with unknown roles.
evidence: Observation from the data shown in Figure 2b-g

claim: Most positive-valence MBONs innervate aversive-memory compartments.
source: By contrast, most positive-valence MBONs (4/6) innervate aversive-memory compartment, and the remainder innervate compartments with unknown roles.
evidence: Observation from the data shown in Figure 2b-g

claim: Aversive learning depresses the synapse between the conditioned odor-KCs and positive-valence MBONs.
source: Right, (i) aversive learning depresses the synapse between the conditioned odor-KCs and positive-valence MBONs (Hige et al., 2015b), skewing the balance towards negative-valence MBONs.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and illustrated in Figure 2h

claim: Decreased conditioned odor drive to inhibitory positive-valence MBONs can disinhibit the negative-valence MBONs.
source: (ii) Decreased conditioned odor drive to inhibitory positive-valence MBONs can disinhibit the negative-valence MBONs.
evidence: Proposed mechanism illustrated in Figure 2h

claim: There is lateral inhibition between MBONs that encode opposite valence.
source: We noted lateral inhibition between some MBONs that promote opposite behaviors: 6 instances of an avoidance-promoting MBON projecting inhibitory synapses (i.e. GABAergic or glutamatergic [Liu and Wilson, 2013]) onto an approach-promoting MBON, and hree instances of an approach-promoting MBON projecting inhibitory synapses onto an avoidance-promoting MBON.
evidence: Observation from the connectome data shown in Figure 2i

claim: We reconstructed all neurons postsynaptic to all 24 MBONs in both the right and left hemispheres.
source: To investigate how downstream circuits could compare the odor drive to positive- and negative-valence MBONs and read out the learned odor valence, we reconstructed all neurons postsynaptic to all 24 MBONs in both the right and left hemispheres (Figure 3a–b, Figure 3—figure supplement Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2a-e and 3a-d, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Description of the EM reconstruction work performed

claim: We identified 167 left and right homologous pairs of neurons that were strongly and reliably connected to MBONs.
source: We identified 167 left and right homologous pairs of neurons that were strongly and reliably connected to MBONs (see Materials and methods for definition of strong and reliable, Figure 3b).
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction analysis

claim: We named the neurons strongly and reliably connected to MBONs MB second-order output neurons (MB2ONs).
source: We named these neurons MB second-order output neurons (MB2ONs).
evidence: Definition of a new neuron class based on connectivity

claim: ORN42a and ORN42b show the strongest response to the innately attractive odor, ethyl acetate.
source: Olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs), ORN42a and ORN42b (Kreher et al., 2008; Kreher et al., 2005) show the strongest response to the innately attractive odor, ethyl acetate.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: An increase in the activity of ORN42a or ORN42b in untrained animals decreases turning.
source: An increase in the activity of ORN42a or ORN42b in untrained animals decreases turning, while a decrease in their activity increases turning (Schulze et al., 2015; Gepner et al., 2015; Hernandez-Nunez et al., 2015), indicating they promote approach of innately attractive odors.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: ORN42a and ORN42b synapse onto PN42a and PN42b, which bifurcate, sending projections to both the MB and the LH.
source: ORN42a and ORN42b synapse onto PN42a and PN42b, which bifurcate, sending projections to both the MB and the LH.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge

claim: We reconstructed all neurons downstream of PN42a and PN42b and identified 22 pairs of LHNs.
source: We therefore reconstructed all neurons downstream of PN42a and PN42b in the same EM volume and identified 22 pairs of LHNs (LHNs, Figure 3a–f, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a-b, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction work

claim: The LHN pathway downstream of PN42b suppresses turning when activated by ORN42b, even in the absence of a functional MB pathway.
source: In both groups, we observed a comparable and significant decrease in turning in response to an increase in ORN42b activity (Figure 3g). This confirms that the LHN pathway downstream of PN42b suppresses turning when activated by ORN42b, even in the absence of a functional MB pathway, and encodes positive valence (Figure 3g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3g

claim: The MB contributes to some aspects of the innate odor response, specifically to turning following a decrease in odor concentration.
source: Interestingly, compared to animals with intact KCs, larvae with silenced KCs responded differently to a reduction in ORN42b activity at the offset of optogenetic activation (Figure 3g). This suggests that the MB contributes to some aspects of the innate odor response, specifically to turning following a decrease in odor concentration (as would occur when the animal is crawling away from an innately attractive odor source).
evidence: Inference from experimental data shown in Figure 3g

claim: Navigation in a gradient of ethyl acetate was less efficient when KCs were silenced.
source: Consistent with this idea, navigation in a gradient of ethyl acetate (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) was less efficient when KCs were silenced.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: Our EM reconstruction revealed direct connections from some MBONs onto 14 LHNs.
source: Our EM reconstruction revealed direct connections from some MBONs onto 14 LHNs, similar to recent findings in the adult Drosophila (Dolan et al., 2018; Figure 3a and e, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3b i).
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction analysis

claim: We observed direct connections from some LHNs onto four MBONs.
source: We also observed direct connections from some LHNs onto four MBONs (Figure 3a and e, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3b,ii-iii) and the convergence of both LHNs and MBONs onto 44 MB2ONs (Figure 3a and e).
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction analysis

claim: We observed the convergence of both LHNs and MBONs onto 44 MB2ONs.
source: We also observed direct connections from some LHNs onto four MBONs (Figure 3a and e, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3b,ii-iii) and the convergence of both LHNs and MBONs onto 44 MB2ONs (Figure 3a and e).
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction analysis

claim: We call the neurons that receive LHN and MBON input, 'Convergence Neurons' (CNs).
source: Collectively, we call the neurons that receive LHN and MBON input, 'Convergence Neurons' (CNs).
evidence: Definition of a new neuron class based on connectivity

claim: MBON-m1 receives cholinergic (excitatory) input from positive-valence MBON-e1.
source: Specifically, MBON-m1 receives cholinergic (excitatory) input from positive-valence MBON-e1 that repress turning and GABAergic (inhibitory) and glutamatergic (likely inhibitory [Liu and Wilson, 2013]) input from negative-valence MBONs that promote turning (MBON-h1, MBON-h2, MBON-i1, Figure 4a).
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 4a

claim: MBON-m1 receives GABAergic (inhibitory) and glutamatergic (likely inhibitory) input from negative-valence MBONs (MBON-h1, MBON-h2, MBON-i1).
source: Specifically, MBON-m1 receives cholinergic (excitatory) input from positive-valence MBON-e1 that repress turning and GABAergic (inhibitory) and glutamatergic (likely inhibitory [Liu and Wilson, 2013]) input from negative-valence MBONs that promote turning (MBON-h1, MBON-h2, MBON-i1, Figure 4a).
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 4a

claim: MBON-m1 was activated by ethyl-acetate, both in the presence, and absence of a functional MB pathway.
source: We found that, on average, across a population of untrained animals, MBON-m1 was activated by ethyl-acetate, both in the presence, and absence of a functional MB pathway (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 2a-b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c

claim: LHNs provide functional excitatory input to MBON-m1.
source: This indicates that LHNs provide functional excitatory input to MBON-m1.
evidence: Inference from the experimental data showing MBON-m1 activation by odor even when KCs are silenced

claim: Odor-evoked responses in MBON-m1 were highly variable across individuals.
source: Interestingly, odor-evoked responses were highly variable across individuals (ranging from inhibition to excitation), even though, on average across individuals the response was excitatory (Figure 4c).
evidence: Observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4c

claim: The MB could be a significant source of inter-individual variability in odor-evoked responses in MBON-m1.
source: Compared to those with silenced KCs, inter-animal variability in animals with a functional MB contributed to a higher fraction of the overall variance in odor response (Figure 4c, and compare the r2 coefficients in Supplementary file 2). This suggests that the MB could be a significant source of inter-individual variability in odor-evoked responses in MBON-m1.
evidence: Inference from statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Optogenetic activation of KCs evoked diverse responses in MBON-m1, from inhibitory to excitatory or no response.
source: Optogenetic activation of KCs evoked diverse responses in MBON-m1, from inhibitory to excitatory or no response (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4d

claim: On average, across the population of untrained animals, there was no significant excitatory response of MBON-m1 to KC activation.
source: Despite this, KC activation did not activate MBON-m1 in many individuals, and on average, across the population of untrained animals, there was no significant excitatory response (i.e. the mean ∂F/F0 is not significantly different from zero).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4d

claim: The amplitude of change of ∂F/F0 in MBON-m1 was significantly higher after, compared to before, KCs activation.
source: Albeit variable, a response to KCs was generally present in MBON-m1: overall, the amplitude of change of ∂F/F0 (i.e. |maximum ∂F/F0 - minimum ∂F/F0 |) was significantly higher after, compared to before, KCs activation.
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4d

claim: MBON-m1 receives both functional inhibitory and excitatory inputs from the MB pathway.
source: These results demonstrate that MBON-m1 receives both functional inhibitory and excitatory inputs from the MB pathway, in accordance with the direct synaptic input it receives from GABAergic, glutamatergic, and cholinergic MBONs, as well as from KCs.
evidence: Conclusion from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4e

claim: MBON-m1 receives direct input from DANs that are activated by aversive stimuli and whose activation paired with odor induces aversive memory.
source: MBON-m1 receives direct input from DANs that are activated by aversive stimuli and whose activation paired with odor induces aversive memory (Eschbach et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Aversive learning would reduce the conditioned-odor drive to the positive-valence MBON-m1.
source: Based on studies in adult Drosophila (Séjourné et al., 2011; Hige et al., 2015a), we predicted that aversive learning would reduce the conditioned-odor drive to the positive-valence MBON-m1.
evidence: Prediction based on prior research in adult Drosophila

claim: The response of MBON-m1 to conditioned odor was significantly decreased after aversive training.
source: We found that the response to conditioned odor was variable across individuals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2d), but on average, we found significantly decreased responses of MBON-m1 to the paired (CS+) and not the unpaired odor (CS-, Figure 5a, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a

claim: Acute optogenetic silencing of MBON-m1 increases turning.
source: To confirm this, we acutely, optogenetically hyperpolarized MBON-m1 with the anion channel-rhodopsin GtACR2 (Govorunova et al., 2015; Mohammad et al., 2017) and found this increased turning (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b

claim: Increasing and decreasing MBON-m1 activity relative to the baseline was sufficient to decrease and increase turning, respectively.
source: Thus, increasing and decreasing MBON-m1 activity relative to the baseline was sufficient to decrease and increase turning, respectively.
evidence: Conclusion from optogenetic activation and inactivation experiments

claim: Silencing MBON-m1 resulted in increased turn-rate compared to controls.
source: Indeed, we found that silencing MBON-m1 resulted in increased turn-rate compared to controls, consistent with the acute inactivation results (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c

claim: Constitutively inactivating just MBON-m1 did not significantly impair odor navigation.
source: Thus, constitutively inactivating just this one neuron type did not significantly impair odor navigation, possibly due to the existence of 10 other similar, partially redundant CN types.
evidence: Observation from experimental data and inference about redundancy

claim: CN-33 receives cholinergic input from positive-valence MBON-e1.
source: Like MBON-m1, it receives cholinergic input from positive-valence MBON-e1, whose activation represses turning and glutamatergic (likely inhibitory) input from negative-valence MBONs whose activation promotes turning (MBON-i1 and MBON-e2, Figure 6a).
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 6a

claim: CN-33 receives glutamatergic (likely inhibitory) input from negative-valence MBONs (MBON-i1 and MBON-e2).
source: Like MBON-m1, it receives cholinergic input from positive-valence MBON-e1, whose activation represses turning and glutamatergic (likely inhibitory) input from negative-valence MBONs whose activation promotes turning (MBON-i1 and MBON-e2, Figure 6a).
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 6a

claim: CN-33 receives input from the same two LHNs downstream of PN42a/PN42b as MBON-m1.
source: It also receives input from the same two LHNs downstream of PN42a/PN42b as MBON-m1 (Figure 6a).
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 6a

claim: The LHN inputs onto CN-33 are functional, and the innately attractive odor activates CN-33 via the LHN pathway, in untrained animals.
source: This indicates that the LHN inputs onto CN-33 are functional, and that the innately attractive odor activates CN-33 via the LHN pathway, in untrained animals, as was the case for MBON-m1.
evidence: Inference from the experimental data showing CN-33 activation by odor even when KCs are silenced

claim: The MB could be a significant source of inter-individual variability in odor-evoked responses of CN-33.
source: In addition, compared to those with silenced KCs, inter-animal variability in animals with a functional MB contributed to a higher fraction of the overall variance in odor response (i.e. compare the r2 coefficients in Supplementary file 2). The MB could therefore be a significant source of inter-individual variability in odor-evoked responses of CN-33.
evidence: Inference from statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Optogenetic activation of KCs evoked inhibitory responses in some individuals, excitatory responses in some, or no response in others for CN-33.
source: Both in vivo or ex vivo, the optogenetic activation of KCs evoked inhibitory responses in some individuals, excitatory responses in some, or no response in others (Figure 6c and d).
evidence: Observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6c and d

claim: On average, across the population of untrained animals, KC activation did not significantly activate CN-33.
source: As was the case for MBON-m1, on average, across the population of untrained animals, KC activation did not significantly activate CN-33 (Figure 6c), but the absolute amplitude of the responses was increased after KC activation as compared to before.
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6c

claim: CN-33 receives functional inhibitory and excitatory input from KCs.
source: This experiment confirms that CN-33 receives functional inhibitory and excitatory input from KCs (Figure 6d).
evidence: Conclusion from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6d

claim: Since CN-33 does not receive any direct KC input but does receive direct MBON input, these functional connections must be indirect and mediated by the MBONs.
source: Since CN-33 does not receive any direct KC input but does receive direct MBON input, these functional connections must be indirect and mediated by the MBONs (and possibly also by MB2ONs that receive input from these MBONs and synapse onto CN-33).
evidence: Inference from anatomical connectivity and functional data

claim: Optogenetic activation of CN-33 decreased turning and increased crawling.
source: We found that optogenetic activation of CN-33 decreased turning and increased crawling (Figure 6e, Figure 6—figure supplement 2a-d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e

claim: Acutely optogenetically hyperpolarizing CN-33 increased turning relative to controls.
source: To confirm this another way, we acutely optogenetically hyperpolarized CN-33 with GtACR2 (Govorunova et al., 2015; Mohammad et al., 2017) and found this increased turning relative to controls (Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e

claim: Increasing and decreasing CN-33 bi-directionally modulates turning.
source: Thus, as was the case for MBON-m1, increasing and decreasing CN-33 bi-directionally modulates turning.
evidence: Conclusion from optogenetic activation and inactivation experiments

claim: Larvae with constitutively hyperpolarized CN-33 completely lost the ability to modulate turning as a function of their orientation in the odor gradient.
source: These larvae completely lost the ability to modulate turning as a function of their orientation in the odor gradient and showed a significant reduction in their ability to approach the attractive odor source (Figure 6f, see Figure 6—figure supplement 2e for control line SS04330).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6f

claim: Larvae with constitutively hyperpolarized CN-33 showed a significant reduction in their ability to approach the attractive odor source.
source: These larvae completely lost the ability to modulate turning as a function of their orientation in the odor gradient and showed a significant reduction in their ability to approach the attractive odor source (Figure 6f, see Figure 6—figure supplement 2e for control line SS04330).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6f

claim: CN-33 contributes to odor approach by modulating turning.
source: These results suggest that CN-33 contributes to odor approach by modulating turning.
evidence: Inference from the experimental results on CN-33 silencing

claim: Innate and learned valences are thought to be encoded in distinct brain areas in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: The innate and learned valences are thought to be encoded in distinct brain areas in both vertebrates (Li and Liberles, 2015; Choi et al., 2011; Sosulski et al., 2011) and invertebrates (Li and Liberles, 2015; Marin et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: In mammals, the olfactory projection neurons (mitral cells) send divergent projections to two parallel higher order centers, the olfactory amygdala and the piriform cortex, implicated in innate and learned behaviors, respectively.
source: In mammals, the olfactory projection neurons (mitral cells) send divergent projections to two parallel higher order centers, the olfactory amygdala and the piriform cortex, implicated in innate and learned behaviors, respectively (Li and Liberles, 2015; Choi et al., 2011; Sosulski et al., 2011; Root et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: In insects the olfactory projection neurons send divergent projections to the lateral horn (LH) and the mushroom body (MB), implicated in innate and learned behaviors, respectively.
source: Likewise, in insects the olfactory projection neurons send divergent projections to the lateral horn (LH) and the mushroom body (MB, [Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002; Gerber and Stocker, 2007; Eichler et al., 2017; Jeanne et al., 2018]), implicated in innate and learned behaviors, respectively (Li and Liberles, 2015; Heimbeck et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2001; Heisenberg, 2003; Turner et al., 2008; Ruta et al., 2010; Parnas et al., 2013; Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b; Dolan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The MB consists of a set of parallel fiber neurons, the Kenyon cells (KCs), that sparsely encode sensory inputs coming from olfactory and other projection neurons (PNs).
source: The MB consists of a set of parallel fiber neurons, the Kenyon cells (KCs), that sparsely encode sensory inputs coming from olfactory and other projection neurons (PNs [Gerber and Stocker, 2007; Honegger et al., 2011; Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014; Hige et al., 2015b])
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: KC axons are tiled into distinct compartments by terminals of modulatory neurons, mainly dopaminergic (DANs).
source: KC axons are tiled into distinct compartments by terminals of modulatory neurons, mainly dopaminergic (DANs [Eichler et al., 2017; Aso et al., 2014a; Mao and Davis, 2009; Takemura et al., 2017]).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: DANs carry information about positive and negative reinforcement and provide teaching signals for memory formation.
source: DANs carry information about positive and negative reinforcement and provide teaching signals for memory formation (Aso et al., 2014a; Schroll et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2012; Aso and Rubin, 2016; Eschbach et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: In each compartment, DANs synapse onto KCs and onto the dendrites of compartment-specific MB output neurons (MBONs).
source: In each compartment, DANs synapse onto KCs and onto the dendrites of compartment-specific MB output neurons (MBONs [Eichler et al., 2017; Takemura et al., 2017]).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: In the adult, individual MBONs have been shown to promote approach or avoidance and encode positive or negative valence, respectively.
source: In the adult, individual MBONs have been shown to promote approach or avoidance and encode positive or negative valence, respectively (Aso et al., 2014b; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Bouzaiane et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Pairing of an odor with a DAN has been shown to selectively depress the conditioned-odor drive to MBONs in that compartment.
source: Pairing of an odor with a DAN has also been shown to selectively depress the conditioned-odor drive to MBONs in that compartment (Séjourné et al., 2011; Hige et al., 2015a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Prior to learning, positive- and negative-valence MBONs are thought to receive a similar odor drive.
source: Prior to learning, positive- and negative-valence MBONs are thought to receive a similar odor drive.
evidence: Established model from prior research

claim: Aversive and appetitive learning depresses the odor drive to positive- and negative-valence MBONs, respectively.
source: Aversive and appetitive learning depresses the odor drive to positive- and negative-valence MBONs, respectively (Aso et al., 2014b; Owald and Waddell, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Learned valence of stimuli is thought to be encoded as a skew in the activity of the population of MBONs.
source: Learned valence of stimuli is therefore thought to be encoded as a skew in the activity of the population of MBONs.
evidence: Inference from the established model of MB function

claim: We identified 62 neurons per brain hemisphere that represent direct points of convergence between the MB and the LH.
source: We identified 62 neurons per brain hemisphere that represent direct points of convergence between the MB and the LH, that fall into a number of different subtypes based on their patterns of MB and LH inputs and potentially encode a number of distinct features (Figure 3e).
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction analysis

claim: One subtype of 10 convergence neurons (CNs) receives excitatory input from positive-valence MB and LH pathways and inhibitory input from negative-valence MB pathways.
source: One subtype of 10 convergence neurons (CNs) receives excitatory input from positive-valence MB and LH pathways and inhibitory input from negative-valence MB pathways.
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction analysis

claim: The 10 CNs encode integrated odor value and regulate turning.
source: These neurons encode integrated odor value (coding for positive value with an increase in their activity) and regulate turning.
evidence: Conclusion from functional experiments on MBON-m1 and CN-33

claim: The 10 CNs are activated by an attractive odor, and when activated they repress turning.
source: They are activated by an attractive odor, and when activated they repress turning.
evidence: Conclusion from functional experiments on MBON-m1 and CN-33

claim: When the 10 CNs are inactivated, they increase turning.
source: Conversely, when inactivated, they increase turning.
evidence: Conclusion from functional experiments on MBON-m1 and CN-33

claim: Learning could potentially skew the balance of excitation and inhibition onto the 10 CNs and thereby modulate turning.
source: Based on this, we speculate that learning could potentially skew the balance of excitation and inhibition onto these neurons and thereby modulate turning.
evidence: Speculation based on the experimental findings

claim: For one of the 10 CNs (MBON-m1), aversive learning skews inputs towards inhibition.
source: For one of these neurons, we indeed verified that aversive learning skews inputs towards inhibition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on MBON-m1 responses after training

claim: Many of the CNs that receive input from both MBONs and LHNs also provide direct or indirect feedback to MB modulatory neurons.
source: We find that many of the CNs that receive input from both MBONs and LHNs also provide direct (including CN-33) or indirect (including MBON-m1) feedback to MB modulatory neurons that provide teaching signals for learning (n = 18).
evidence: Result from the EM reconstruction analysis

claim: At least some of the feedback connections from CNs to modulatory neurons are functional and can influence memory formation.
source: In a former study (Eschbach et al., 2020), we have shown that at least some of these feedback connections are functional and can influence memory formation.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: CN-33/FAN-7 is capable of generating an olfactory memory when it is paired with an odor.
source: For example, CN-33/FAN-7 is capable of generating an olfactory memory when it is paired with an odor.
evidence: Inference from prior research on CN-33/FAN-7

claim: A major role of the CNs may be not only to organize current actions, but also to regulate learning.
source: A major role of the CNs discovered in this study may therefore be not only to organize current actions, but also to regulate learning.
evidence: Speculation based on the connectivity and functional properties of CNs
